posts.title: 700 PHP Packages Backdoored in 15 Minutes
posts.author: admin
posts.excerpt: Last Friday night, an attacker rewrote 700 versions of widely-used PHP packages in under fifteen minutes. Any developer who ran a routine dependency update during the hours that followed unknowingly handed over their AWS keys, GitHub tokens, SSH keys, and crypto wallet recovery phrases. This is what a software supply chain attack looks like in practice — and why your vendor's code is now your security problem.
posts.content:
Last Friday night, someone with push access to the Laravel-Lang GitHub organization rewrote every git tag across four widely-used PHP packages in under fifteen minutes. For the roughly fourteen hours that followed, any developer who ran composer install or composer update unknowingly had credential-stealing malware delivered to their machine. The packages — laravel-lang/lang, laravel-lang/attributes, laravel-lang/http-statuses, and laravel-lang/actions — are community-maintained localization libraries with millions of downloads and a long track record of being exactly the kind of boring, stable dependency nobody thinks twice about. That reputation is precisely what made them such a good target.

The attack mechanics are worth understanding, because they reveal something important about how supply chain attacks work. Rather than publishing a suspicious new version that might trigger automated alerts, the attacker rewrote the historical git tags — version 1.0, version 2.3, whatever — to point at newly malicious commits. When a developer pulled down what looked like a trusted, stable old release, they were getting a poisoned package that wired a helper file into PHP's autoloader, running it on every request the moment the package was installed. That helper reached out to a remote server and pulled down a Windows binary that went straight to work: AWS credentials, GitHub tokens, Stripe secrets, Kubernetes configs, SSH keys, .env files, crypto wallet recovery phrases — if it was on the developer's system and looked like a secret, it left.

Here is what makes this matter outside the world of PHP development: nobody on an affected team did anything wrong. No one clicked a phishing link. No one used a weak password. The malware arrived through the exact mechanism developers are supposed to use to manage their software. If your company runs any application built on Laravel, or if any of your vendors do, you may have been affected without a single person on your team making a mistake. Supply chain attacks are effective precisely because they weaponize trust. The attacker was not breaking in — they were walking through a door your security checklist never thought to lock.

The window of exposure ran from approximately 10:32 PM UTC on May 22 to midday on May 23. Any environment that ran composer operations during that period should be treated as compromised: rotate every credential you can identify, audit cloud access logs, and assume that anything stored in environment variables was exfiltrated. The packages themselves have since been restored, but credentials do not become safe just because the attack is over.

What this incident illustrates — again, for anyone keeping count — is that a strong perimeter does not protect you from a compromised supply chain. Firewalls, access controls, and security training are all necessary, but they share a blind spot: they assume the software itself is trustworthy. Auditing your software supply chain, understanding where your dependencies come from, and knowing whether you would detect a tampering event before it costs you — these are genuinely hard problems, and they require specialized expertise that most organizations do not have in-house. The teams that get caught in attacks like this are, almost without exception, the ones who believed that was someone else's job.

posts.title: MFA Won't Stop Kali365
posts.author: admin
posts.excerpt: The FBI just flagged a phishing service called Kali365 that bypasses multi-factor authentication — not by cracking it, but by exploiting Microsoft's own authentication flow against you. It's already compromising hundreds of Microsoft 365 accounts daily across healthcare, finance, and government. Here's how it works and why 'we have MFA' is no longer a complete answer.
posts.content:
The FBI doesn't typically issue public service announcements about specific cybercrime tools unless those tools are already causing serious, widespread damage. On May 21, they made that call for Kali365 — a phishing-as-a-service platform that has been compromising Microsoft 365 accounts across healthcare, manufacturing, finance, and government, sometimes at hundreds of organizations per day.

The reason Kali365 is worth understanding isn't just that it exists — plenty of phishing kits do. It's that it specifically defeats multi-factor authentication. Not by breaking MFA, but by working around it in a way that exploits legitimate infrastructure Microsoft built for entirely reasonable purposes. The technique is called device code phishing. It exploits the OAuth authentication flow Microsoft designed to allow devices like smart TVs and printers to log in to accounts — situations where typing a full password isn't practical. In that flow, a user receives a short code and is directed to a real Microsoft verification page. No fake login form. No spoofed website. They authenticate on genuine Microsoft infrastructure. MFA fires. It succeeds. And the attacker, who initiated the authentication request in the first place, collects the OAuth access and refresh tokens that Microsoft issues afterward. At that point, they have persistent access to Outlook, Teams, and OneDrive — no password on file, no further MFA prompts ever required.

What Kali365 does is productize this attack. For $250 a month per target, someone with no real technical skill can rent the infrastructure, AI-generated phishing lures, automated campaign dashboards, and token capture capabilities needed to run this at scale. Arctic Wolf and Proofpoint documented hundreds of compromises in April 2026 alone, and the kit had only launched that month. The phishing email typically impersonates something familiar — a cloud service notification, a document share, a collaboration invite — and the only ask is that the user visit a real Microsoft URL and enter a code. The whole attack happens in plain sight on legitimate infrastructure.

The uncomfortable truth is that a lot of organizations treat enabling MFA as the finish line. It isn't, and Kali365 isn't the first tool to demonstrate this. Device code phishing has been documented as a technique for years; what changes is when it gets packaged into a cheap, accessible service that lowers the skill floor to almost nothing. The people getting hit aren't doing anything obviously wrong. The attack is specifically designed to look like a routine authentication request.

Defense here isn't exotic. Microsoft's Conditional Access policies can block device code flow entirely for users who don't require it, which is most people in most organizations. Device code authentication should be disabled by default in corporate environments — and it rarely is, because it requires someone to understand what it is, care about the risk, and make a deliberate configuration change. Monitoring for anomalous OAuth token grants, training employees to be skeptical of authentication prompts they didn't initiate, and reviewing token lifespans can all help close the gap. The distance between 'we use Microsoft 365' and 'our Microsoft 365 is actually configured securely' is where Kali365 is operating, and it's profitable. Closing that gap requires someone who knows exactly what to look for — and that's work worth doing before the FBI starts sending more personal notices.

posts.title: Six Million Victims, One Deceived Employee
posts.author: admin
posts.excerpt: Carnival Corporation sent breach notifications to nearly six million people after an attacker used social engineering to deceive a single employee into granting system access. Names, addresses, passport numbers, and government IDs are now in criminal hands — and not one firewall could have stopped it.
posts.content:
Carnival Corporation sent breach notification letters on May 27 to nearly six million people informing them that their names, addresses, dates of birth, phone numbers, email addresses, and government-issued ID numbers had been stolen — including, for many, passport numbers. The world’s largest cruise line operator didn’t lose this data because someone exploited a zero-day or brute-forced a password. It lost it because an attacker convinced one of their employees to hand over access.

That’s what social engineering looks like at scale. On April 14, an unauthorized actor used social engineering to deceive a Carnival employee and gain access to a portion of the company’s internal IT environment. By April 22, the company had determined that personal data had been illegally copied. Social engineering is the polite term for manipulation: presenting yourself as someone with legitimate authority, making an unusual request feel routine, exploiting the natural human tendency to help a colleague or comply with someone who sounds like they know what they’re talking about. It requires no technical knowledge, no malware, no exploit code. The ShinyHunters extortion group, which later claimed responsibility, has made a consistent practice of this approach against large organizations — not because technical defenses are easy to defeat, but because human ones rarely are.

What makes this breach particularly serious is the durability of what was taken. Passport numbers are not like passwords. You cannot reset a passport in two minutes with an account recovery flow. Government-issued IDs are effectively permanent identifiers — once in criminal hands they can be used in identity fraud schemes, false documentation, or financial crime for years. The nearly six million people receiving those Carnival letters now have a shadow over their most durable personal identifiers, regardless of whether they ever cruise again.

The uncomfortable truth for every organization reading this is that Carnival’s security team was probably not negligent in any particularly interesting way. They almost certainly had firewalls, endpoint protection, network monitoring, and access controls. None of it mattered when one employee had a convincing conversation with the wrong person. Human beings are the variable in every security equation that doesn’t respond to a patch or a configuration change. Security training helps, but it is not a complete defense — and the organizations that discover this the hard way tend to be the ones that assumed training alone was sufficient.

The structural fix isn’t to distrust your employees. It’s to design systems where a single deceived person cannot become the pivot point for six million records leaving the building. That means strict need-to-know access controls, requiring multi-party authorization for bulk data operations, and monitoring for data movement that doesn’t fit normal patterns — before exfiltration becomes a log entry nobody caught rather than a breach nobody stopped. For most organizations, implementing those controls correctly requires someone who understands the attack surface from the inside. Carnival had the resources to build that infrastructure. Most businesses are working from a much thinner baseline, which makes the gap between a social engineering attempt and a successful one narrower than they’d probably like to believe.
